content.text:
**Candidate 7** has the highest expected profit. I worked this out by hand on the forecast (mean) values without simulating, so the confidence is moderate.

1. **Daily ordering costs too much.** Candidate 2 orders almost every day. That adds about 12–13 extra order days at 41 each, roughly 500 in extra cost. Its smaller stock does not make up for that.

2. **Ordering every 2 days fits both products.** Product 0 can be sold for 6 days and product 1 for 4, so stock left over after two days usually sells later instead of being written off. For product 0 a missing unit costs 11 (lost margin 4 plus penalty 7), while a spare unit costs only storage. So it pays to order generously, and product 1 behaves the same way.

3. **The 240-unit warehouse limit is the main constraint.** Under the every-2-days plans, both products arrive on the same odd days. On day 15 a large product 0 order (160–165 units, placed on day 12) arrives together with product 1 (53–69 units), plus whatever is left over. In candidates 0, 4 and 6 that total is close to or above 240. When that happens, some of product 1 is lost on arrival even though it was already paid for. Candidates 0 and 6 also come close to the limit on other days because their orders are the largest.

4. **Candidate 7 handles the day-16 spike best.** Demand for product 0 jumps to 121 on day 16. Candidate 7 splits that supply: 43 units arrive on day 15 and 139 units arrive on day 16, a day when product 1 does not arrive. This avoids the overflow at the cost of one extra order fee of 41. Its other quantities sit between the moderate and the generous plans.

5. **Candidate 5 is short at the spike and risks overflow.** It orders every 3 days, which saves about 5 order fees. But on day 15 its 175 units of product 0 arrive while about 61 units of product 1 are still in stock. That totals about 236, so any extra leftover overflows. Those 175 units must also cover expected demand of about 199 over days 15–17, so it is likely to run short and pay penalties.

I pick **candidate 0**, but with only moderate confidence. The runner-up is candidate 7, and the gap between them is smaller than the noise in my rough estimates. I worked this out by hand and did not simulate it.

**Cutting the field down.**
- **Candidate 2** orders every day. That is about 27 fixed fees of 41 instead of 14, so roughly 530 more spent on fees. That is a clear loss.
- **Candidate 5** orders every three days, which saves about 200 in fees. But the stock it holds is higher. Around day 15, product 0 (up to 175 units) plus product 1 comes close to the 240 limit, and in a high-demand stretch an arrival may not fit. The bigger stock also adds holding cost. The fee saving does not clearly outweigh these.
- The rest (0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7) all order every other day. They differ mainly in how much they order relative to the forecast.

**Product 0** (lost sale costs 4 margin + 7 penalty = 11; shelf life 6 days, so extra stock carries over to the next cycle): ordering above the mean pays off. Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, so the order needs a margin of roughly ×1.2–1.3 on top of the forecast.
- Candidates 1, 3 and 4 order about ×1.0–1.1, which means frequent shortages at 11 each.
- Candidate 7 orders about ×1.15.
- Candidate 0 orders about ×1.25 and candidate 6 about ×1.3.

**Product 1** (lost sale costs 6; a wasted unit costs 12 plus holding): the target is about 0.9 of actual mean demand.
- Candidates 0 and 4 have identical product 1 orders, about 0.95 × forecast. That fits the target.
- Candidates 1 and 3 order too little (about 0.8–0.85).
- Candidate 6 orders too much (about 1.04).

**Storage limit.** Both products arrive on the same odd days. Around day 15 (the order for the 121-unit demand on day 16):
- Candidate 0 gets 160 + 63 units plus leftovers, about 250, so roughly 10 units of product 1 may be lost.
- Candidate 6 overflows more.
- Candidate 7 avoids the problem by splitting the order and bringing 139 in on day 16. But it pays an extra fee and orders less of product 0 overall.

**Bottom line.** Candidate 0 has the best mix: a product 0 cushion of about ×1.25 and the right product 1 level. Its overflow loss at day 15 is small. Candidate 7 handles day 16 better but should lose more over the run to product 0 shortages. Candidate 6 overflows more and over-orders product 1.

**Выбор: кандидат 4**, но уверенность низкая. Я считал всё в уме и приближённо; кандидаты 0, 6 и 7 близки к нему, и ошибка вполне возможна. Отказ (−1) тоже был бы обоснованным выбором.

**Слабые кандидаты отсеиваются сразу:**
- **Кандидат 2** заказывает каждый день. Это примерно 27 фиксированных платежей по 41 вместо 13–14, то есть около 570 лишних расходов.
- **Кандидат 1** заказывает ровно по прогнозу, а среднее множителя около 1,046. Поэтому нехватки товара 0 будут почти постоянными, а каждая недостающая единица стоит 4 упущенной маржи плюс 7 неустойки, итого 11.
- **Кандидат 3** заказывает товар 1 по ×0,8. Нехватка единицы товара 1 стоит около 6 (3 маржи плюс 3 неустойки). Списание бывает редко: при цикле 2 дня и годности 4 дня остаток продаётся в следующем цикле.
- **Кандидат 5** работает циклом 3 дня. Он экономит около 4 платежей по 41, но держит большие запасы и рискует переполнением склада.

**Сравнение оставшихся (общий спрос: товар 0 — около 1414 за дни 0–29; товар 1 — около 860 за дни 5–29, с учётом множителя 1,046):**

| Кандидат | Поставки товара 0 (со стартовыми 51) | Поставки товара 1 | Главная проблема |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | ≈1400, около среднего спроса | ≈782 | Нехватки обоих товаров, лишь небольшой перелив на пике (день 15) |
| 0 | ≈1558 | ≈782 | Растущий излишек товара 0, переполнение склада |
| 6 | ≈1618 | ≈862 | Переполнение склада |
| 7 | ≈1470 | ≈740 | Недобор товара 1 |

- **Переполнение склада.** В нечётные дни приходят оба товара сразу. У кандидата 6 приходы в дни 21, 23 и 27 составляют около 200–220 единиц ещё до учёта остатков. Склад вмещает 240, товар 0 принимается первым, поэтому пропадает уже оплаченный товар 1. У кандидата 0 похожая картина. Кроме того, у него копится излишек товара 0, на который идут хранение и списания, примерно −600…−1000 в сумме.
- **Кандидат 7.** Отдельный заказ в день 13 снимает проблему вместимости на пике дня 16 и даёт больше товара 0. Но он стоит лишние 41, а товар 1 у него недозаказан примерно на 42 единицы по сравнению с кандидатом 4, это около −250. По моей грубой оценке, это перевешивает выигрыш по товару 0, около +95.
- **Кандидат 4** лучше других балансирует нехватки и переполнение, хотя тоже недобирает товара 1.

I pick **candidate 7**, but with only moderate confidence. I worked it out by hand from the rules and the forecast, without a simulation, and it is close to candidate 0.

**Ruled out first:**
- **Candidate 2** orders every day. That means about 27 fixed fees of 41 instead of about 13, roughly 575 extra, which daily ordering can't win back.
- **Candidate 5** orders every 3 days. On day 15 it receives 175 units of product 0 and 115 of product 1, which is over the 240 capacity, so it loses stock it has already paid for. Product 1 also expires after 4 days, so more of it gets thrown out.
- **Candidates 1 and 3** under-order. For product 0, a missing unit costs 11 (lost margin 4 plus penalty 7), while a spare unit costs little because it keeps 6 days and carries over. Ordering just at the forecast (candidate 1) is also too low because the average demand multiplier is 1.046, not 1. Candidate 3 adds a ×0.8 factor on product 1, which leads to frequent shortages.

**The demand peak decides between the rest.** Day 16 has a forecast of 121 for product 0. In candidates 0, 4 and 6, the day-12 order of 160–165 units of product 0 arrives on day 15, the same day as a product 1 delivery of about 60–70 units. Add what is still on the shelf and the total is about 250 or more, over the 240 limit. Since product 0 is accepted first, roughly 10–15 units of product 1 are lost, worth about 120–150 already paid, plus later shortages.

Candidate 7 splits that order: 43 units arrive on day 15 and 139 on day 16, when no product 1 arrives. The extra order costs 41, but it avoids the overflow. It also gives 182 units for the 158 forecast over days 15–16, close to its normal ×1.15 margin.

**Candidate 7 vs. candidate 0:** Candidate 0 buys more product 0 (×1.25) and slightly more product 1 (×0.95). That means more storage cost but fewer shortages, which roughly cancels out. So candidate 7's main edge is the peak handling, worth an estimated 60–110. Candidate 6 (×1.3 / ×1.05) has the same overflow problem and pays more for storage and expired product 1.

**Выбор: кандидат 0.** Всё посчитано в уме, грубо, на прогнозных значениях. Ниже приблизительные оценки, а не симуляция.

**Что одинаково у всех.** В дни 1–3 нехватка товара 0, а в дни 1–4 — товара 1, потому что первые поставки приходят только в день 3 и в день 5. Стартовый запас товара 1 к тому же списывается вечером дня 3. Эти потери от плана не зависят. Отличие начинается с дня 3.

**Чем дешевле ошибаться.**
- Товар 0: если не хватило единицы, теряем 11 (маржа 4 + неустойка 7). Лишняя единица стоит около 0,3 в день. Годность 6 дней, поэтому остаток почти всегда продаётся в следующем цикле. Значит, товар 0 выгодно заказывать с хорошим запасом.
- Товар 1: нехватка единицы стоит 6 (маржа 3 + неустойка 3). При цикле 2 дня и годности 4 дня остаток продаётся первым в следующем цикле. Поэтому лишняя единица обходится только хранением 0,5–1. Множитель около 0,95 лучше, чем 0,8–0,9.

**Где теряет каждый кандидат.**
- **Кандидат 5 (цикл 3 дня):** в день 15 приходит 175 + 115 = 290 единиц при вместимости 240. Излишек пропадает уже оплаченным, хранение тоже выше. Отпадает.
- **Кандидат 2 (заказ каждый день):** около 13 лишних платежей по 41, то есть примерно 530. Отпадает.
- **Кандидаты 1 и 3:** товара 0 заказано мало, а нехватка стоит 11 за единицу. У кандидата 3 ещё и товар 1 урезан до ×0,8. Частые неустойки.
- **Кандидат 6:** в утро дня 15 приходит 165 единиц товара 0, 69 товара 1, плюс остатки — около 265 при вместимости 240. Пропадает около 25 единиц товара 1, это примерно по 12 за единицу плюс упущенные продажи.
- **Кандидат 4:** вместимость в целом выдерживает, но запаса по товару 0 мало (×1,1), поэтому при всплесках спроса будут неустойки.
- **Кандидат 7:** пик дня 16 продуман хорошо, отдельный заказ в день 13 стоит лишних 41. Но запас по товару 0 ниже (×1,15), и товар 1 урезан до ×0,9.
- **Кандидат 0:** самый большой запас по товару 0 (×1,25) и товар 1 ×0,95. Переполнение грозит только в день 15: около 248 при 240, теряется порядка 8 единиц товара 1. В день 27 загрузка на грани, около 241. Потери в конце горизонта небольшие.

**Устойчивость к случайности.** Множитель спроса в среднем 1,046, а разброс по дням около 30 %. В таких условиях больший запас по дорогому в нехватке товару 0 защищает лучше всего. Ожидаемая выгода кандидата 0 перекрывает его небольшой перелив в день 15. Ближайший соперник — кандидат 7.

**Ответ: кандидат 7.** Уверенность умеренная: кандидаты 0, 4 и 7, по моей оценке, расходятся всего на ~100–200. Считал в уме, на прогнозных значениях, без симуляции.

1. **Отсев по фиксированным платежам.**
   - Кандидат 2 заказывает почти каждый день. Это ~27 платежей по 41 против 14 у двухдневных планов, лишних примерно 530. Малые списания это не окупают.
   - У кандидата 5 трёхдневные партии крупные: до 175 + 115 = 290 при вместимости 240. Остатки копятся сильнее, а товар 1 годен всего 4 дня. Перелив и списания здесь вероятнее, чем у двухдневных планов.

2. **Склад переполняется на пике.** В двухдневных планах товар 0 заказан в день t и приходит в t+3, товар 1 приходит в t+5. Поэтому оба товара всегда приходят в один и тот же нечётный день. Под пик дня 16 (прогноз 121) у кандидатов 0, 4 и 6 в день 15 приходит товар 0 (160–165) и товар 1 (66–72). Вместе с остатками это больше 240. Товар 1 принимается вторым, поэтому теряется именно он: он уже оплачен по 12, и вдобавок получается его нехватка. У кандидата 0 с запасом ×1.25 остатки товара 0 растут, и та же опасность повторяется к концу горизонта (около дня 27).

3. **Почему именно 7.** Он делит пиковую закупку товара 0: 43 в день 13 (приход 15-го) и 139 в день 14 (приход 16-го). На складе получается примерно 83 + 70 в день 15 и около 220 в день 16, то есть перелива нет, а цена этому — один лишний платёж 41.
   - Коэффициент ×1.15 по товару 0 — середина между ×1.1 и ×1.25. Это разумно: нехватка обходится в 11 за единицу, а излишек почти полностью переходит дальше и стоит в основном хранения по 0,3 в день.

4. **Минус кандидата 7.** Товар 1 у него заказан скупо (×0.9 при среднем множителе 1,046), поэтому нехваток по товару 1 будет немного больше. По моей оценке, это меньше потерь от перелива у конкурентов.

**Choice: candidate 7.** Candidate 7 should come out roughly 50–100 ahead of candidate 4, its closest rival. All figures are rough mental estimates, so this is a lean, not a large margin.

**Losses every plan shares:**
- The opening stock runs short and no plan can fix it. Product 0 has 51 units against about 118 demand on days 0–2. Product 1 has 39 against about 140 on days 0–4.
- Candidate 2 orders every day, so it pays the 41 fixed fee about 27 times instead of about 13. That costs roughly 550 extra and puts it behind the two-day-cycle plans.
- Candidate 5 orders every 3 days. Product 1 keeps only 4 days, so this plan writes off more product 1 at 12 per unit and fills the 240-unit warehouse more often.

**How much product 0 to order.** A unit short costs 11 (margin 4 plus penalty 7). A unit too many usually carries over to the next cycle, so it mostly costs storage. Demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. That makes ordering about ×1.1–1.15 of the forecast the right level.
- Candidates 0 and 6 order ×1.25–1.3. The surplus builds up, spoils after 6 days, and makes the warehouse overflow more likely.
- Candidate 1 orders ×1.0, so it runs short often and pays the penalty of 7 each time.

**How much product 1 to order.** A unit short costs 6. A leftover unit can still be sold in the next cycle, because a batch sells for 4 days. That makes ordering about ×0.95 of the forecast sensible.
- Candidate 3 orders ×0.8, which is too little. Candidate 1 orders ×0.85, also low.
- Candidate 7 orders ×0.9. That should cost it about 130 against candidate 4's ×0.95.

**Candidate 4 against candidate 7:**
- On product 0, candidate 7 orders ×1.15 against candidate 4's ×1.1. That should gain it about 115.
- On product 1, candidate 7 gives back about 130, as above.
- At the peak (121 demand on day 16), candidate 4 fills the warehouse on the morning of day 15. It receives 165 of product 0 and 63 of product 1, plus about 20 units left over. That is about 248 against room for 240, so roughly 8 units of product 1 are lost after being paid for, at about 100 total.
- Candidate 7 splits the peak order across day 12 (43 units) and day 13 (139 units). It avoids the overflow and covers the peak more fully (182 against 165). The extra 41 fee is more than paid back.
- Candidate 0 also overflows on day 15 (160 + 63 + a larger leftover) and over-orders product 0.

Net: candidate 7 trades a small product 1 loss for a product 0 gain plus the peak handling, so it comes out ahead.

I'd pick **candidate 7**, but not by a wide margin: it is the expected-value favourite, and its closest rival is candidate 4. I worked this out by hand with rough estimates, without simulating anything.

**Same for every plan:**
- **The first three days are short regardless.** The opening stock of item 0 (51 units) can't cover days 0–2 (demand 39 + 32 + 47 = 118), and nothing ordered can arrive before day 3.
- **Ordering daily is too expensive.** Candidate 2 orders every day, which costs about 14 × 41 ≈ 570 more in order fees than ordering every other day. Lower holding and spoilage don't make up that difference.
- **Ordering every third day is worse.** Candidate 5 holds three days of stock at once, which runs into the 240-unit cap, raises holding costs and lets item 1 spoil.

**Item 0** (a shortage costs about 11 per unit; leftovers carry over for up to 6 days):
- Since every quantity is fixed in advance, any surplus adds up from one order to the next and eventually spoils.
- **Orders about 25–30% above forecast are wasteful.** Candidates 0 and 6 do this. They buy roughly 13–18 extra units per order, which spoil at 4 each, totalling about 700–1000. That is much more than the shortage costs they avoid.
- **Orders at forecast run short.** Candidate 1 does this and leaves a steady shortfall of around 100 units, costing about 1100.
- **About 1.1–1.15 × forecast is best.** Candidates 3, 4 and 7 order at this level.

**Item 1** (a missed unit loses 15 + 3; it spoils after 4 days):
- **Ordering below the true average costs about 6 per missed unit.** Candidate 3 orders about 0.8 × forecast and candidate 1 about 0.86, which costs them several hundred.
- **Around 0.9–1.05 × forecast** (candidates 0, 4, 6 and 7) works out about the same.

**The deciding factor is day 15:**
- Day 16 has a demand spike of 121, and the large item-0 order placed on day 12 lands on day 15. Item 1 also arrives that day, and item 0 is accepted into the warehouse first.
- **Candidate 4:** about 165 incoming plus roughly 40 left over brings item 0 to about 205. Only about 35 spaces remain for item 1, so about 30 or more of the 66 units arriving are lost. Those units would almost all have sold, so the cost is roughly 500.
- **Candidates 0 and 6** overflow even more on that day.
- **Candidate 7** splits the order into 43 on day 12 and 139 on day 13, so the bulk arrives on day 16, exactly when the spike hits. Its warehouse stays at about 210 or below. The cost is one extra order fee (41) and slightly lower item-1 orders (about −200).

Candidate 7 still comes out ahead of candidate 4 by roughly 250. That is real but uncertain, because it depends on how much item 0 builds up before day 15. Even so, I'm confident enough to choose rather than answer "don't know".

Я выбираю **кандидата 7**. Перевес над кандидатами 0 и 4 небольшой: это прикидка в уме, а не точный прогон.

**Почему не кандидаты 5 и 2.**
- **Кандидат 5 (цикл 3 дня).** Дней с заказом 9 вместо 14, это экономия около 205. Но товар в среднем лежит на складе на полночи дольше, и хранение растёт примерно на 420. Кроме того, 175 единиц товара 0 (приход в день 15) не закрывают дни 15–17 со спросом около 199. Утром дня 15 склад почти полон: остаётся около 61 единицы товара 1 с прихода дня 14. Поэтому часть товара 0 пропадает, а на пике спроса 121 будет нехватка с неустойкой 7.
- **Кандидат 2 (заказ каждый день).** Около 27 платежей по 41, это примерно на 530 больше, чем при цикле 2 дня. Хранение экономит только около 420, так что в сумме план проигрывает.

**Циклы по 2 дня (кандидаты 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7).**
- **Товар 0.** Нехватка стоит 11 за единицу (маржа 4 плюс неустойка 7). Излишек обходится дёшево: он переходит в следующий цикл, срок годности 6 дней. Но план фиксирован заранее, и при запасе 1,25–1,3 при среднем множителе 1,046 излишек копится и в итоге списывается по 4 за единицу плюс хранение. Поэтому запас около 1,1–1,15 выглядит лучшим балансом.
- **Товар 1.** Нехватка стоит 6, а списание 12 и больше, поэтому лучше заказывать скупо: 0,9–0,95.
- **Кандидаты 1 и 3** заказывают слишком мало: частые нехватки товара 0.
- **Кандидат 6** даёт 1,3 по товару 0 и 1,05 по товару 1. Утром дня 15 склад переполняется: 165 единиц товара 0, около 69 товара 1 и остатки. Пропадает товар 1 по 12 за единицу, плюс списания из-за избыточного заказа.
- **Кандидат 0** (1,25 по товару 0) теряет в основном на списаниях накопленного излишка, на пике небольшой перелив.
- **Кандидат 4** (1,1 по товару 0) остаётся с меньшим запасом против колебаний спроса.

**Кандидат 7** заказывает товар 0 с запасом 1,15, товар 1 по 0,9. Заказ под пик 121 разделён: 43 единицы приходят в день 15, 139 в день 16. Склад не упирается во вместимость, на день пика запас около 145 при ожидаемом спросе около 127. Лишний платёж 41 это окупает. При отклонении спроса от прогноза этот план выглядит самым устойчивым.

Я не смог уверенно выбрать лучший план, поэтому возвращаю **choice = -1** («не знаю»). Расчёт был грубым и в уме. Сильнейшие кандидаты расходятся по ожидаемой прибыли меньше, чем меняется результат от случайного спроса.

**Слабее остальных:**
- **Кандидат 1** (×1.0 по товару 0). Неустойка 7 плюс упущенная маржа 4 дают 11 на единицу нехватки, а при среднем множителе 1,046 нехватка будет постоянной.
- **Кандидат 3** (×0.8 по товару 1). Каждая нехватка стоит 6 (маржа 3 + неустойка 3), а остаток почти всегда успевает продаться в следующем цикле.
- **Кандидат 2.** Около 27 фиксированных платежей по 41, это примерно на 570 больше, чем у двухдневных планов. Меньшие списания этого не покрывают.
- **Кандидат 6** (×1.3 / ×1.05). Оба товара приходят в одни и те же нечётные дни. Например, 165 + 72 = 237 единиц в день 15 при вместимости 240, так что товар 1, который принимается вторым, частично пропадает. Систематический излишек товара 0 к тому же списывается через 6 дней.

**Близкие кандидаты: 0, 4, 7 и, возможно, 5.**
- **Кандидат 0** (×1.25 / ×1.0) лучше защищён от нехватки товара 0. Зато излишек над средним спросом (около 20 %) накапливается и списывается, а в пик дня 16 он даёт только 160 единиц.
- **Кандидат 7** (×1.15 / ×0.9) заказывает пик дня 16 отдельно в день 13 и так обходит ограничение склада. Ожидаемая нехватка в пике у него примерно на 4 единицы меньше, это около 44, что почти съедается лишним платежом 41. Товара 1 он берёт чуть меньше выгодного.

По моим оценкам, разница между 0, 4 и 7 — несколько десятков, а случайный спрос сдвигает итог на сотни. Поэтому разумной уверенности нет.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I'm only moderately confident, and the estimate is rough: I worked it out in my head from average demand, without a full day-by-day simulation.

**Why candidate 7:**

That gives 182 units for days 15–16 against forecast demand of 158. Candidates 0/3/4/6 bring 160–165 units in one delivery on day 15. That is thin cover for the spike, and they pay to store the extra units for a day.
- **Warehouse capacity (240).** In the plans that order every two days, both products often arrive on the same odd-numbered day. On day 15, candidate 6 receives 165 + 69 units, plus about 25–35 left over. Roughly 30 units of product 1 are lost, at 12 each. Candidate 0 loses about 8 units and candidate 4 about 13. Day 27 is also tight for 6 and 0. Candidate 7 stays under the limit everywhere (day 15: 43 + 59 + leftovers; day 27: 127 + 65).
- **Order sizes are a reasonable middle.** Candidate 7's product 0 orders are about 1.14 × forecast. A shortage costs 11 per unit (margin plus penalty), while a surplus carries over to the next cycle, so generous orders pay off. But in a fixed plan surplus piles up and goes to waste after 6 days. Candidates 1 and 3 order too little, especially of product 1 (about 0.8–0.86 × forecast, while average demand is 1.046 × forecast). Candidates 6 and 0 hit the capacity limit.
- **The extra order day costs only 41,** less than the spike shortages and capacity losses it avoids.

**The other candidates:**
- **Candidate 2** orders every day: 27 order days, about 530 more in fees than the others. It also has almost no safety stock, so shortage penalties would be frequent.
- **Candidate 5** orders every three days and saves about 200 in fees. But its order of 175 units on day 12 covers days 15–17, where forecast demand is 199. That's a shortage of 24 units or more just at the average, at 11 per unit. Its product 1 cover is also thin.

I pick **candidate 7**. This is a mental estimate, not a full step-by-step simulation, so the gaps between the top plans are approximate.

**How each lot is costed**
- **Product 0** has a margin of 4 and a penalty of 7, so each unit short costs about 11. A unit left over is cheap: it carries into the next cycle and only costs holding (0.3 per day). It is written off only after 6 days. Ordering a bit above forecast therefore pays off.
- **Avoid ordering too far above forecast.** The plan is fixed and does not adjust to what is left over. With an average multiplier of about 1.046, a ×1.25–1.3 order builds up about 20% surplus every cycle. That surplus piles up, gets written off at 4 per unit, and fills the 240-unit warehouse.
- **Product 1** has a short shelf life (4 days) and a shortage cost of only 3+3=6. Ordering at about ×0.9–0.95 is right.

**Comparing the plans**
- **Candidate 2:** about 27 fixed charges of 41 each, so roughly 1,100 goes on fees alone. This is clearly worse.
- **Candidate 5:** a 3-day cycle with large lots of product 1, which only lasts 4 days. This means write-offs, high holding costs and warehouse overflow.
- **Candidates 1 and 3:** they order too little. Shortages of product 0 cost 11 per unit, and the multiplier averages above 1.
- **Candidates 0 and 6:** ×1.25–1.3 on product 0 builds surplus that spoils and overflows. On top of that, their peak order on day 12 is capped at 160–165 to cover 158 units of demand (days 15–16). That leaves almost no buffer at exactly the most expensive point.
- **Candidate 4:** the peak is covered by one lot of 165 arriving on day 15 (×1.04 only). The same morning, 63 units of product 1 arrive, so some of product 1 is lost to the 240-unit cap.
- **Candidate 7:** a sensible ×1.15 / ×0.9 overall. It also places a separate order on day 13 (139 units arriving on day 16) under the 121-unit peak. That gives a buffer of about 15% with no overflow: on day 16 morning stock is about 185 of 240, at the cost of one extra 41. This plan is also the most robust if demand comes in above forecast.

I'd pick **candidate 7**. I worked this out by reasoning through the rules, not by simulating every day, so the comparison is approximate.

**Product 0.** A shortage costs 11 per unit: the lost margin of 4 plus the penalty of 7. Over-ordering is cheap. A batch keeps for 6 days and orders come every 2 days, so leftovers sell in the next cycle and mostly cost only 0.3 a day in storage. Some safety margin over the forecast pays off, especially since the average demand multiplier is about 1.046. Too much margin, though, turns into steady write-offs at 4 per unit. The ×1.25–1.3 plans (candidates 0 and 6) push this too far, and they also take up warehouse space ahead of product 1.

**Product 1.** A shortage costs 6 (3 margin + 3 penalty), while an expired unit loses 12 and keeps for only 4 days. A modest ×0.9–0.95 is reasonable.

**The deciding factor: the day-16 peak (121 units of product 0).**
- In the 2-day-cycle plans, the day-12 order has to cover days 15 and 16 together. The forecast is 37 + 121 = 158, about 165 with the 1.046 mean multiplier.
- Candidates 3 and 4 order 165, which is no safety margin. Candidates 0 and 1 order 160, which is below expected demand. Candidate 6's 165 is also its lowest margin of the run. The likely result is a shortage of about 15–20 units at 11 each.
- On top of that, on day 15 the 165 units of product 0 arrive together with about 63 units of product 1, plus leftovers. That likely goes over the 240 capacity, and because product 0 is accepted first, the paid-for product 1 is what spills.
- Candidate 7 splits the peak: 43 units arrive on day 15 and 139 on day 16, about 182 in total (×1.15). It doesn't hit the capacity limit on either day and has a real safety margin on the peak. The cost is one extra 41-unit order fee, which is clearly less than the losses it avoids.

**The other plans.**
- Candidate 2 pays about 27 order fees of 41 each.
- Candidate 5 runs a 3-day cycle. Product 1 keeps only 4 days, so it will see write-offs at 12 per unit, and it has a higher risk of overflowing the warehouse.
- Candidates 1 and 3 order too little, so shortage penalties will be frequent.

Candidate 7 also holds up best if actual demand differs from the forecast. It has a moderate margin on both products, the peak is covered without overflow, and none of its risks get much worse when demand swings.

I picked **candidate 4**, with only moderate confidence. Candidates 4, 0, 6 and 7 are close, and I worked this out by hand with no simulation.

**How the plans are built.** Candidates 0, 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7 all order every other day. Each product 0 order covers 2 days of demand starting 3 days later, and each product 1 order covers 2 days starting 5 days later. They differ mainly in how big the orders are compared with the forecast.

| Candidate | Product 0 vs forecast | Product 1 vs forecast |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~1.0× | ~0.86× |
| 3 | ~1.1× | ~0.82× |
| 7 | ~1.14× | ~0.9× |
| 4 | ~1.1× | ~0.95–1.0× |
| 0 | ~1.25× | ~0.95–1.0× |
| 6 | ~1.3× | ~1.05× |

**Why candidate 4:**
- **Product 0.** Running out costs 4 lost margin plus a 7 penalty, about 11 per unit. A spare unit costs little because it keeps for 6 days and sells in the next 2-day window. Average demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast, so 1.1× gives a small, sensible margin. At 1.25–1.3× (candidates 0 and 6), the surplus builds up and expires. It also crowds the warehouse.
- **Product 1.** A shortage costs about 6 per unit (3 margin plus 3 penalty). Since orders are fixed in advance, ordering above average demand piles up stock that expires, so ordering near average demand is about right. Candidate 4 sits there. Candidates 1, 3 and 7 order 10–18% less and keep running short: for candidate 7 that's roughly 9 units per cycle, about 650 over the month.
- **Warehouse limit (240).** Both products arrive on the same odd days, and product 0 is accepted first. In candidate 6 (and partly in 0), arrivals of 190–220 plus leftovers on days 21–27 go over 240. The product 1 units that don't fit are already paid for (12 each) and are lost.
- **Day 16 demand spike (121).** In candidate 4, day 15 brings about 228 units plus leftovers, which is close to the limit, but expected losses are small. Candidate 7 avoids this by splitting the order, but it orders too little of product 1 overall.
- **Candidates 2 and 5.** Candidate 2 orders almost every day, which adds about 25 × 41 ≈ 1000 in daily order fees. Candidate 5 orders every 3 days in large batches, which regularly goes over the warehouse limit, and product 1 expires after 4 days.
